Shelemiah
shel-e-mī´ah
n. (a priest made treasurer by Nehemiah; and several men of Jeremiah's day; Hebrew Shelemyah)
Hebrew Shelemyah, ‘the LORD is recompense’ or ‘whom the LORD repays’ — from shalam, to be complete, to make good, to requite.

Biblical Definition

Shelemiah is a name carried by several men in the last books of the Old Testament, and the most instructive is the priest Nehemiah appointed over the treasuries. Having found the house of God forsaken and the Levites fled to their fields for want of their portions, Nehemiah set treasurers over the stores — “Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah… for they were counted faithful” (Neh 13:13). That is the whole reason given for the appointment, and it is the only qualification named. Others of the name stand in Jeremiah's narrative on both sides. Jehudi, sent to fetch Baruch's roll before the princes, is a son of Shelemiah's line (Jer 36:14); and it was Irijah the son of Shelemiah, a captain of the ward, who seized Jeremiah in the gate of Benjamin and charged him with falling away to the Chaldeans (Jer 37:13). A Shelemiah is also the father of Hananiah who repaired a piece of the wall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not enter Shelemiah; the name is fixed by the Hebrew text as, the LORD is recompense.

expand to see more

The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.

SHELEMIAH. A priest whom Nehemiah made treasurer over the treasuries of the house of God.

The name signifies, Jehovah is recompense, or repayment.

Several men of this name appear in the history of Jeremiah.

It is a compound of shalam, to requite or make good, with the divine name.

Key Scripture

Neh 13:13 — "And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren."

Neh 3:30 — "After him repaired Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, another piece. After him repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber."

Jer 36:14 — "Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them."

Jer 37:13 — "And when he was in the gate of Benjamin, a captain of the ward was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah; and he took Jeremiah the prophet, saying, Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans."

Modern Corruption

Faithfulness is treated as the modest virtue left when ability is lacking, though Nehemiah names it as the entire qualification for handling the church's money.

expand to see more

Nehemiah 13:13 gives one reason for the appointment of these treasurers: they were counted faithful. Not that they were skilled accountants, not that they were prominent, not that they were owed a post — they were reckoned trustworthy, and that settled it. The common instinct is to treat faithfulness as the consolation quality, the thing said of a man when nothing more impressive can be said. Scripture inverts this. It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, and the Lord's own commendation on the last day is not well done, thou brilliant servant.

The principle to recover is what this appointment was for. The Levites had abandoned the house of God because the portions had not been delivered — a failure of administration had emptied the temple of its ministers. Nehemiah's remedy was not a new law but trustworthy men whose office was to distribute unto their brethren. Honest handling of ordinary money is a spiritual office, and its neglect scatters a congregation as surely as false doctrine. The two Shelemiahs of Jeremiah's day are a useful contrast: one line produced a man who fetched the prophet's roll, another produced the captain who arrested the prophet at the gate. The name meant the LORD recompenses. He does, both ways.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shelemyah (H8018), the LORD is recompense; from shalam (H7999), to be complete, to requite, to make good.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shelemyah (H8018) — Shelemiah; Nehemiah 13:13, Jeremiah 36:14, Jeremiah 37:13.

Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be safe, complete, to recompense or repay.

Hebrew aman (H539) — to be faithful, trustworthy; the root behind, counted faithful.

Hebrew otsar (H214) — a treasury, storehouse; Nehemiah 13:12-13.

The same root shalam yields shalom, peace, and the peace offering.

Usage

"“For they were counted faithful” — the whole stated qualification."

"“Their office was to distribute unto their brethren” — stewardship as ministry."

"“Irijah the son of Shelemiah… took Jeremiah” — the name on the other side."
